docs.title: ursus: DataFrames for Go
docs.text:
A dataframe library for Go, modelled on Polars. Lazy queries with a query optimizer, Apache Arrow memory, SIMD kernels, and execution that spills to disk instead of running out of memory. Pure Go: no cgo, no C++ toolchain, no Python.

Get started Coming from Polars API reference

go get github.com/advenn/ursus

df, err := ursus.ScanCSV("testdata/sales.csv").
    Filter(ursus.Col("qty").Gt(int64(3))).
    GroupBy(ursus.Col("region")).
    Agg(
        ursus.Col("qty").Mul(ursus.Col("price")).Sum().Alias("revenue"),
        ursus.Len().Alias("orders"),
    ).
    Sort(ursus.Desc(ursus.Col("revenue"))).
    Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df)
Output
shape: (3, 3)
┌─────────┬─────────┬────────┐
│ region  │ revenue │ orders │
│ String  │ Float64 │ Uint64 │
├─────────┼─────────┼────────┤
│ "south" │ 46.5    │ 3      │
│ "north" │ 30.75   │ 2      │
│ "east"  │ 18      │ 1      │
└─────────┴─────────┴────────┘

Nothing runs until Collect. The optimizer reads only the columns the query uses, the group-by runs on every core, and the same query runs under a memory limit by spilling to disk.

  • Lazy and optimized

    A query is a plan until it is collected. Filters and projections are pushed into the scans and through joins, constants are folded, and a subtree used twice runs once.

    Lazy and eager

  • Polars' expressions, in Go

    Col("qty").Mul(Col("price")).Sum().Over(Col("region")): the same expressions, contexts and names as Polars, checked against Polars' answers on the same inputs.

    Expressions

  • Out of core

    Sort, group-by, join, unique and window functions spill to disk under a memory limit and give the answer they give in memory. An operator that cannot spill fails with an error naming itself.

    Memory and spilling

  • Pure Go

    go get is the whole install. It cross-compiles and links into a static binary like any other Go dependency, and Go functions run inside a query as UDFs.

    Installation

  • Parquet, CSV and Arrow

    Read and write Parquet and CSV from files, memory, or any io.ReaderAt, with row groups pruned by statistics. Arrow records go in and out, zero-copy out.

    Quick start

  • Checked against other engines

    Every TPC-H (PDS-H) and h2o.ai benchmark answer is validated against DuckDB's, and the test suite runs at four SIMD widths and with SIMD off.

    Benchmarks

docs.title: Is ursus for you?
docs.text:
It is pure Go, and that is the reason to pick it. The cost should be just as plain: ursus is slower than the serious analytical engines. On the h2o.ai benchmark at ten million rows it takes about 1.3 times Polars' time over Parquet and 1.6 times over CSV; on TPC-H at scale factor 1, about 2 times.

A good fit:

  • data that fits comfortably in memory, up to tens of millions of rows, where the difference is half a second against a tenth of one;
  • a Go service that needs real dataframe work, joins, group-bys and window functions, and cannot take on cgo, a Python sidecar or a large C++ dependency to get it;
  • anywhere the deployment story is worth more than the last multiple of speed.

Not a good fit:

  • interactive analytics over hundreds of millions of rows: use DuckDB or Polars;
  • anywhere you can link cgo freely: duckdb-go is a binding to a mature engine and about twice as fast on TPC-H;
  • anything production-critical today. ursus is at 0.6, and its API still changes between releases, as the changelog records.

docs.title: Benchmarks
docs.text:
ursus is slower than Polars and DuckDB, and says by how much. Everything that measures it lives in bench/: TPC-H (as Polars' PDS-H) and the h2o.ai database-like suite, against DuckDB, Polars, pandas, DataFusion, chDB, Arrow-Go, Gota and QFrame.

Every answer is validated against DuckDB's, and an engine that answers wrongly is struck through in the report rather than reported as a fast number. ursus passes all 22 PDS-H queries and all 15 h2o.ai queries.

docs.title: Against Polars
docs.text:
Geometric means over each suite's queries, ursus and Polars run together in one session on 8 threads:

Suite ursus Polars ursus / Polars h2o.ai, 10M rows, Parquet 697 ms 531 ms 1.3× h2o.ai, 10M rows, CSV 1,784 ms 1,088 ms 1.6× TPC-H, scale factor 1 158 ms 79 ms 2.0× TPC-H, scale factor 0.1 20 ms 9 ms 2.3× TPC-H SF=1, peak memory 0.83 GB 0.92 GB 0.9×

Over the releases, ursus's time against Polars' has come down from 3.3× to 1.3× on h2o.ai over Parquet, and from 10.8× to 2.0× on TPC-H at scale factor 1.

docs.title: How they were taken
docs.text:
The figures are v0.6.4's, from a laptop under real conditions, so a small difference is noise and the ordering is the signal. Later 0.6 releases changed no plan the suites run, which a byte-for-byte diff of all 37 queries' optimized plans checks at each release, so the figures stand. The full report, with every engine, every query, the caveats and peak memory, is bench/results/REPORT.md.

To run them yourself:

cd bench
make preflight   # refuses to run without the free memory it needs
make setup
make bench       # generate, compute DuckDB's answers, run, validate, report

docs.title: Expressions
docs.text: An expression says how to compute a column: Col("qty").Mul(Col("price")). It holds no data, and it is computed only where a query puts it. The same expression gives a column per row in Select and WithColumns, one value per group in Agg, and keeps rows in Filter. These are Polars' contexts, and ursus follows them.

docs.title: The same expression, three ways
docs.text:
ctx := context.Background()
revenue := ursus.Col("qty").Mul(ursus.Col("price"))

perRow, err := sales().Select(ursus.Col("order_id"), revenue.Alias("revenue")).Head(3).Collect(ctx)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
total, err := sales().Select(revenue.Sum().Alias("revenue")).Collect(ctx)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
byRegion, err := sales().GroupBy(ursus.Col("region")).
    Agg(revenue.Sum().Alias("revenue")).
    Sort(ursus.Asc(ursus.Col("region"))).Collect(ctx)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(perRow)
fmt.Println(total)
fmt.Println(byRegion)
Output
shape: (3, 2)
┌──────────┬─────────┐
│ order_id │ revenue │
│ Int64    │ Float64 │
├──────────┼─────────┤
│ 1        │ 15      │
│ 2        │ 6       │
│ 3        │ 15.75   │
└──────────┴─────────┘

shape: (1, 1)
┌─────────┐
│ revenue │
│ Float64 │
├─────────┤
│ 108.75  │
└─────────┘

shape: (3, 2)
┌─────────┬─────────┐
│ region  │ revenue │
│ String  │ Float64 │
├─────────┼─────────┤
│ "east"  │ 22.5    │
│ "north" │ 39.75   │
│ "south" │ 46.5    │
└─────────┴─────────┘
  • in a Select of row-wise expressions, revenue is a value per row;
  • its Sum() is an aggregate: in a Select it is one value for the frame;
  • in GroupBy(...).Agg, the same aggregate is one value per group.

GroupBy() with no keys also aggregates the whole frame, as one group.

docs.title: Windows: an aggregate beside the rows
docs.text:
Over computes an expression within each group of rows and gives the answer back on every row of the group, so the frame keeps its height. A sum over a region beside each order, and each order's rank within its region:

df, err := sales().
    Select(
        ursus.Col("order_id"),
        ursus.Col("region"),
        ursus.Col("qty"),
        ursus.Col("qty").Sum().Over(ursus.Col("region")).Alias("region_qty"),
        ursus.Col("qty").Rank(ursus.RankDense, true).Over(ursus.Col("region")).Alias("rank"),
    ).
    Sort(ursus.Asc(ursus.Col("region")), ursus.Asc(ursus.Col("rank"))).
    Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df)
Output
shape: (8, 5)
┌──────────┬─────────┬───────┬────────────┬────────┐
│ order_id │ region  │ qty   │ region_qty │ rank   │
│ Int64    │ String  │ Int64 │ Int128     │ Uint32 │
├──────────┼─────────┼───────┼────────────┼────────┤
│ 6        │ "east"  │ 12    │ 14         │ 1      │
│ 4        │ "east"  │ 2     │ 14         │ 2      │
│ 1        │ "north" │ 10    │ 20         │ 1      │
│ 3        │ "north" │ 7     │ 20         │ 2      │
│ 7        │ "north" │ 3     │ 20         │ 3      │
│ 5        │ "south" │ 9     │ 19         │ 1      │
│ 8        │ "south" │ 6     │ 19         │ 2      │
│ 2        │ "south" │ 4     │ 19         │ 3      │
└──────────┴─────────┴───────┴────────────┴────────┘

Window functions include the cumulative ones (CumSum, CumMax, ...), Shift, Diff, Rank, RollingMean and the other rolling windows by rows or by time, and the exponentially weighted EwmMean and its kin.

docs.title: Many columns at once
docs.text:
Col takes several names, and All() and Exclude(...) select by what to leave out. An expression over several columns is one expression per column, and Suffix or Prefix names them:

df, err := sales().
    Select(ursus.Col("product"), ursus.Col("qty", "price").Mul(int64(2)).Suffix("_x2")).
    Head(3).
    Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df)
Output
shape: (3, 3)
┌─────────┬────────┬──────────┐
│ product │ qty_x2 │ price_x2 │
│ String  │ Int64  │ Float64  │
├─────────┼────────┼──────────┤
│ "apple" │ 20     │ 3        │
│ "apple" │ 8      │ 3        │
│ "pear"  │ 14     │ 4.5      │
└─────────┴────────┴──────────┘

docs.title: Namespaces
docs.text:
Methods for one kind of column sit behind a namespace:

Namespace For For example Str() text Contains, Replace, Split, ToUpper, Strptime, Slice Dt() dates and times Year, Weekday, Truncate, OffsetBy, ConvertTimeZone List() lists Len, Get, Contains, Sum, Eval, Sort, Unique Struct() structs Field, WithFields, RenameFields, JsonEncode Bin() binary Contains, StartsWith, Encode, Size Cat() enums GetCategories, LenBytes, Slice 
df, err := sales().
    Select(
        ursus.Col("product").Str().ToUpper().Alias("product"),
        ursus.Col("date").Dt().Weekday().Alias("weekday"),
        ursus.Col("product").Str().Contains("p", true).Alias("has_p"),
    ).
    Head(3).
    Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df)
Output
shape: (3, 3)
┌─────────┬─────────┬───────┐
│ product │ weekday │ has_p │
│ String  │ Int32   │ Bool  │
├─────────┼─────────┼───────┤
│ "APPLE" │ 6       │ true  │
│ "APPLE" │ 6       │ true  │
│ "PEAR"  │ 7       │ true  │
└─────────┴─────────┴───────┘

docs.title: Conditions
docs.text:
When(cond).Then(a).Otherwise(b) is a conditional column, and When may follow Then for further conditions, the first true one winning:

ursus.When(ursus.Col("qty").Ge(10)).Then("large").
    When(ursus.Col("qty").Ge(5)).Then("medium").
    Otherwise("small")

Comparisons give a Bool column, combined with And, Or and Not under SQL's three-valued logic: null.And(false) is false, and null.And(true) is null.

docs.title: Literals
docs.text:
A Go value is a literal wherever an expression goes: Col("qty").Gt(3), Then("bulk"), FillNullWith(0.0). Lit(v) makes a literal expression of its own, and a Go slice is a List literal.

A literal has its Go value's type. A Go integer constant is an int, an Int64, and a float constant a Float64, so Col("a").Add(3) of an Int32 column is an Int64 column, and Col("f").Mul(2.5) of a Float32 one a Float64. Write Add(int32(3)) to stay at Int32. Polars' literals take the column's type instead. The fills are the exception: FillNullWith, FillNan and their kin meet the column, so FillNullWith(0) of an Int32 column stays Int32, and only a float fill widens an integer column.

docs.title: Names
docs.text: An expression is named after the leftmost column it reads: Col("qty").Mul(Col("price")) is named qty. Alias names it, and goes last, since an alias inside an expression does not name the whole.

docs.title: A query is a plan
docs.text:
A LazyFrame is a query, not data. ScanCSV, Filter, GroupBy and the rest each add a step to a plan, and nothing is read or computed until the plan runs:

  • Collect(ctx) runs it and gives a DataFrame, the answer, held in memory;
  • CollectBatches(ctx) runs it and gives the answer a batch at a time;
  • Count(ctx) runs it and gives the number of rows;
  • WriteParquet(ctx, w) and WriteCSV(ctx, w) run it into a writer.

Because the whole query is known before it runs, ursus can check it first and then rewrite it.

docs.title: Checked before it runs
docs.text:
When a query is collected, ursus resolves every column's type, expands each selection of several columns, and type-checks every expression, before any data is read. A mistake is reported then, with what was meant:

lf := sales().
    Select(ursus.Col("prodcut")). // a typo: nothing has run, so nothing fails yet
    Filter(ursus.Col("qty").Gt(int64(3)))

_, err := lf.Collect(context.Background())
fmt.Println(err)
Output
ursus: select: unknown column "prodcut"
  did you mean: "product"?
  available: order_id, date, region, product, qty, price
  at Project

The Select with the typo did not fail when it was written. A query being built never fails: the first error is kept, the chain goes on, and Collect returns it. So a long chain has one if err != nil, at the end.

docs.title: Rewritten before it runs
docs.text:
The optimizer rewrites the plan into one that gives the same answer for less work:

  • predicate pushdown: a filter moves toward the scan, through joins, so fewer rows travel;
  • projection pushdown: a scan reads only the columns the query uses;
  • limit and top-k pushdown: a Head after a Sort becomes a top-k;
  • constant folding and simplification;
  • common subplans: a subtree used twice runs once.

Explain shows the plan. Optimized(false) shows it as written:

q := sales().
    Filter(ursus.Col("qty").Gt(int64(3))).
    Select(ursus.Col("product"), ursus.Col("qty"))

written, err := q.Explain(context.Background(), ursus.Optimized(false))
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(written)
Output
PROJECT [col("product"), col("qty")]
  FILTER [(col("qty") > lit(3))]
    CSV SCAN testdata/sales.csv
      projection: * (6 cols)

and without the option, the plan that runs. The PROJECT is gone, and the scan reads two of six columns:

plan, err := ursus.ScanCSV("testdata/sales.csv").
    Filter(ursus.Col("qty").Gt(int64(3))).
    Select(ursus.Col("product"), ursus.Col("qty")).
    Explain(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(plan)
Output
FILTER [(col("qty") > lit(3))]
  CSV SCAN testdata/sales.csv
    projection: [product, qty] (2/6 cols)

Explain's output is stable on purpose: ursus's own tests compare plans as text, so a query that still gives the right answer while reading forty columns instead of two fails a test.

docs.title: Eager: a DataFrame
docs.text:
A DataFrame is an answer in memory, Arrow arrays underneath. Its methods mirror LazyFrame's, and each is a lazy query over the frame, collected at once. So each takes a context, which can cancel it:

ctx := context.Background()
df, err := sales().Collect(ctx)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
big, err := df.Filter(ctx, ursus.Col("qty").Ge(int64(9)))
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(big.Shape())
Output
3 6

df.Lazy() turns a frame back into a query, for a chain of several steps optimized together.

docs.title: Streaming the answer
docs.text:
CollectBatches is a Go iterator over the answer's batches, so an answer larger than memory never has to be held at once:

ctx := context.Background()
for batch, err := range sales().CollectBatches(ctx, ursus.WithBatchSize(3)) {
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    fmt.Println("a batch of", batch.Height(), "rows")
}
Output
a batch of 3 rows
a batch of 3 rows
a batch of 2 rows

Breaking out of the loop stops the query and removes any spill files it wrote.

docs.title: Order and threads
docs.text:
A query runs on every core by default; WithThreads(n) sets how many. A scan's rows come in the file's order at any thread count, a filter keeps its input's order, and a sort's is sorted. Two orders are not promised, as in Polars, and each has an option that promises one:

  • a group-by's groups: MaintainOrder() gives them in the order their keys first appear;
  • an inner join's rows, which follow whichever input ursus did not hash: JoinMaintainOrder(true) keeps the left frame's order.

docs.title: Memory and spilling
docs.text: A query in ursus runs under a memory budget. When the operators that hold data across batches, a sort, a group-by, a join's build side, reach it, they write what they hold to disk and carry on, and the answer is the one they give in memory. An operator that cannot spill fails at the budget with an error naming itself, instead of growing until the operating system kills the process.

docs.title: The default budget
docs.text:
A query with no limit of its own is budgeted at half the memory the process can have: the smaller of its container's limit and the machine's memory on Linux, and the machine's memory on macOS and Windows. Half, because ursus's buffers live on the Go heap, which grows to about twice what is live before it collects.

Under that default, ursus also sets the Go runtime's soft memory limit near the same ceiling, so the heap's slack stays under it. GOMEMLIMIT, or calling ursus.LeaveProcessMemoryLimit() before the first query, keeps a program's own choice.

docs.title: A limit of your own
docs.text:
WithMemoryLimit sets the budget for one query, WithSpillDir where its files go, and WithMemoryStats reports what it held and how many files it wrote. A group-by over 25,000 keys under 256 KiB:

keys := make([]int64, 100_000)
for i := range keys {
    keys[i] = int64(i * 7919 % 25_000)
}
var stats ursus.MemoryStats
df, err := ursus.Frame(ursus.Values("k", keys)).
    GroupBy(ursus.Col("k")).Agg(ursus.Len().Alias("n")).
    Select(ursus.Len().Alias("groups"), ursus.Col("n").Max().Alias("largest")).
    Collect(context.Background(),
        ursus.WithMemoryLimit(256<<10),
        ursus.WithSpillDir(os.TempDir()),
        ursus.WithMemoryStats(&stats))
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df)
fmt.Println("spilled:", stats.Spills > 0)
Output
shape: (1, 2)
┌────────┬─────────┐
│ groups │ largest │
│ Uint64 │ Uint64  │
├────────┼─────────┤
│ 25000  │ 4       │
└────────┴─────────┘

spilled: true

The spill files are removed when the query ends, on success, on an error, and when a loop over CollectBatches breaks early. WithMemoryLimit(0) turns the budget off.

docs.title: What spills
docs.text:
• sort, and a top-k with any k;
  • group-by, including the values a median, a quantile or an NUnique holds;
  • join, both sides partitioned;
  • unique;
  • window functions, over many partitions or one huge one;
  • keyed Rolling and GroupByDynamic;
  • tail and reverse.

JoinAsOf, MergeSorted and HStack stream their input, as Rolling and GroupByDynamic do, so they hold little to begin with.

docs.title: What does not
docs.text:
A few answers are as large as their input, and cannot be divided across files: Implode holds every value of a group as its answer, for one. Each such operator fails at the budget, and its error says what it holds, why it cannot spill, and what the alternatives are:

keys := make([]int64, 100_000)
_, err := ursus.Frame(ursus.Values("k", keys)).
    Select(ursus.Col("k").Implode()).
    Collect(context.Background(), ursus.WithMemoryLimit(64<<10), ursus.WithSpillDir(os.TempDir()))
fmt.Println(err)
Output
ursus: group_by: memory limit of 64.0KiB exceeded: the query is holding 105.2KiB, 105.2KiB of it in this operator
  group_by holds one entry per distinct key, and implode holds every VALUE as its answer — which partitioning to disk cannot divide, because it divides across keys (quantile, median and n_unique spill their values); raise the limit with WithMemoryLimit
  sort, group_by, join, unique, over, reverse and tail spill to disk; join_asof, merge_sorted, hstack, rolling and group_by_dynamic stream their input; an over computing a rolling window by time one of whose periods holds more than the limit fails rather than exceed it, and so does implode over one group larger than it

Collect itself holds its whole answer, by definition. An answer larger than memory goes through CollectBatches, or WriteParquet and WriteCSV, which stream it.

docs.title: A larger-than-memory query
docs.text:
A sort of more Parquet than fits in memory, written to a file as it comes out of the sort, holding at most 512 MiB:

ctx := context.Background()
err := ursus.ScanParquet("events/*.parquet").
    Sort(ursus.Desc(ursus.Col("ts"))).
    SinkParquet(ctx, "sorted.parquet",
        ursus.WithMemoryLimit(512<<20),
        ursus.WithSpillDir("/var/tmp/ursus"))
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

Each path that spills is tested under a limit far below its input, against its answer without one.

docs.title: Types and nulls
docs.text:
Every column has one type, and a frame's schema is its columns' names and types, known before a query runs:

df, err := sales().Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df.Schema())
Output
{order_id: Int64, date: Date, region: String, product: String, qty: Int64, price: Float64}

docs.title: The types
docs.text:
Type Go value Notes Bool bool Int8 … Int64, Uint8 … Uint64 int8 … uint64 Int128 ursus.Int128Value what an integer sum gives Float32, Float64 float32, float64 Decimal(p, s) 128-bit; exact +, -, * and Sum, refused past 38 digits String, Binary string, []byte Date time.Time a calendar day Datetime(unit, zone) time.Time a unit of s, ms, us or ns, and an IANA zone or none Duration(unit) time.Duration TimeOf(unit) a time of day Enum(...) string fixed categories, sorted in their order List(T) a slice a list of values a row StructOf(fields...) a struct named fields a row

ursus.Int64, ursus.Date and the rest name the types, and Datetime, Duration, TimeOf, Decimal, List, Enum and StructOf make one. A type is a comparable value, so it can key a map.

docs.title: Null is not NaN
docs.text:
Null is a missing value, and any type can hold one. NaN is a float that is not a number, the answer to 0.0 / 0.0. They are different, and ursus keeps them apart everywhere:

df, err := ursus.Frame(
    ursus.ValuesNullable("x", []float64{1, math.NaN(), 0}, []bool{true, true, false}),
).Select(
    ursus.Col("x"),
    ursus.Col("x").IsNull().Alias("is_null"),
    ursus.Col("x").IsNan().Alias("is_nan"),
).Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df)
Output
shape: (3, 3)
┌─────────┬─────────┬────────┐
│ x       │ is_null │ is_nan │
│ Float64 │ Bool    │ Bool   │
├─────────┼─────────┼────────┤
│ 1       │ false   │ false  │
│ NaN     │ false   │ true   │
│ null    │ true    │ null   │
└─────────┴─────────┴────────┘

A null's test is IsNull, a NaN's IsNan; FillNull and FillNan repair them, and DropNulls and DropNans drop their rows.

docs.title: Nulls in aggregates
docs.text:
An aggregate skips nulls. Count counts the values that are there, Len the rows, and a mean is the sum of the values over their count, not over the rows:

df, err := ursus.Frame(
    ursus.ValuesNullable("score", []float64{4, 0, 8}, []bool{true, false, true}),
).Select(
    ursus.Len().Alias("rows"),
    ursus.Col("score").Count().Alias("count"),
    ursus.Col("score").NullCount().Alias("nulls"),
    ursus.Col("score").Mean().Alias("mean"),
    ursus.Col("score").FillNullWith(0.0).Mean().Alias("mean_as_zero"),
).Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df)
Output
shape: (1, 5)
┌────────┬────────┬────────┬─────────┬──────────────┐
│ rows   │ count  │ nulls  │ mean    │ mean_as_zero │
│ Uint64 │ Uint64 │ Uint64 │ Float64 │ Float64      │
├────────┼────────┼────────┼─────────┼──────────────┤
│ 3      │ 2      │ 1      │ 6       │ 4            │
└────────┴────────┴────────┴─────────┴──────────────┘

Two rules follow SQL rather than Polars, because a null can become a number but a number cannot become a null again:

  • the Sum of a group with no values is null, not 0;
  • the Mean of a group with no values is null, not NaN.

docs.title: Casts
docs.text:
Cast converts a column to another type and refuses a value it cannot convert, naming it. CastLossy turns such values into nulls instead:

ctx := context.Background()
text := ursus.Frame(ursus.Values("n", []string{"12", "7", "seven"}))

_, err := text.Select(ursus.Col("n").Cast(ursus.Int64)).Collect(ctx)
fmt.Println(err)

df, err := text.Select(ursus.Col("n").CastLossy(ursus.Int64)).Collect(ctx)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df)
Output
ursus: cast: cannot parse "seven" as Int64 at row 2
  use CastLossy to turn unparseable values into nulls instead
shape: (3, 1)
┌───────┐
│ n     │
│ Int64 │
├───────┤
│ 12    │
│ 7     │
│ null  │
└───────┘

A cast never loses a value silently: an integer that does not fit a narrower type is refused by Cast, and a float rounds only when the target is a float.

docs.title: Values from Go
docs.text:
ursus.Values makes a column from a slice of a Go type, []time.Time a Datetime(ns, "UTC") one, and ursus.ValuesNullable one with nulls, from the values and whether each is present.

Going the other way, a null never comes back as a zero mistaken for a value:

  • df.At[T](row, name) and a Series[T]'s Get give the value and whether it is present;
  • df.Rows[T]() decodes a null into a pointer field as nil; declare the field *int64 where a column can be null.

docs.title: Coming from Polars
docs.text:
ursus is modelled on Polars: the same expressions, the same contexts, mostly the same names, and its answers are tested against Polars 1.44's on the same inputs. What changes is what Go asks for.

Polars (Python)ursus (Go) 
import polars as pl

df = (
    pl.scan_csv("sales.csv")
    .filter(pl.col("qty") > 3)
    .group_by("region")
    .agg(
        (pl.col("qty") * pl.col("price")).sum().alias("revenue"),
        pl.len().alias("orders"),
    )
    .sort("revenue", descending=True)
    .collect()
)

df, err := ursus.ScanCSV("sales.csv").
    Filter(ursus.Col("qty").Gt(3)).
    GroupBy(ursus.Col("region")).
    Agg(
        ursus.Col("qty").Mul(ursus.Col("price")).Sum().Alias("revenue"),
        ursus.Len().Alias("orders"),
    ).
    Sort(ursus.Desc(ursus.Col("revenue"))).
    Collect(ctx)

docs.title: What Go changes
docs.text:
• Methods, not operators. Go has no operator overloading, so pl.col("a") > 3 is Col("a").Gt(3), and a * b is a.Mul(b).
  • Lazy is the real API. A LazyFrame is a query and Collect runs it. A DataFrame's methods are a lazy query collected at once, so each takes a context.Context: df.Filter(ctx, pred).
  • Errors come at the end. A query being built never fails: an unknown column or a type mismatch is kept and returned by Collect, with a hint, so a chain stays a chain.
  • Values come back typed. df.Column[int64]("qty") is a Series[int64], and df.Rows[Sale]() a []Sale, through Go 1.27's generic methods.
  • Options are functions. Join(other, JoinOn(Col("k")), JoinHow(JoinLeft)) where Polars takes keyword arguments.

docs.title: Where ursus answers differently
docs.text:
These are deliberate, and each is documented beside the method:

  • An integer sum is an Int128, as DuckDB's is, so it cannot overflow. Polars' sum of Int64 is an Int64.
  • The sum of an all-null group is null, not 0, and its product null, not 1: a null can be filled with 0 afterwards, but a 0 cannot be told from a real one.
  • Count(ctx) of a frame is its number of rows. Polars' frame count() is each column's non-null count; in ursus that is Select(ursus.All().Count()).
  • NUnique does not count null as a value; Polars counts it.
  • Round rounds half away from zero; Polars rounds half to even, which RoundHalfToEven selects.
  • Max and Min propagate NaN; Polars' max ignores it, and its nan_max propagates it, as NanMax does here.
  • A literal has its Go value's type: Col("a").Add(3) of an Int32 column is an Int64, since a Go integer constant is an int; write int32(3) to keep Int32. Polars' literals take the column's type, as a fill value's does here.
  • Div and Pow always give a float.
  • An expression is named after its leftmost column. Col("a").Alias("x").Add(1) is x in Polars and a here: put the alias last.
  • Cut and Hist give text, where Polars gives a Categorical, which ursus does not have yet.
  • A Time takes a unit, where Polars' is nanoseconds.

The full list, with the step that made each choice, is in feature-gaps.md §9, and what Polars has that ursus does not yet is in the rest of that file.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
go get github.com/advenn/ursus

That is the whole install. ursus is pure Go, with Apache Arrow's Go library as its one direct dependency besides golang.org/x/text: no cgo, no C or C++ toolchain, no Python runtime and no sidecar process. It cross-compiles like any other Go module.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Go 1.27 or newer. Two of its changes are load-bearing:

  • generic methods are why df.Column[int64]("qty"), df.Rows[Sale]() and Series[T].Map[U] exist at all;
  • a generic method still cannot satisfy an interface, so every public type is a concrete struct, and the polymorphism is kept in unexported interfaces.

docs.title: Your first program
docs.text:
Make a module and add ursus to it:

mkdir hello && cd hello
go mod init hello
go get github.com/advenn/ursus

Put this in main.go and go run .:

main.go
package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "log"

    "github.com/advenn/ursus"
)

func main() {
    df, err := ursus.Frame(
        ursus.Values("name", []string{"ursus", "polars", "pandas"}),
        ursus.Values("language", []string{"Go", "Rust", "Python"}),
    ).Filter(ursus.Col("language").Eq("Go")).Collect(context.Background())
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    fmt.Println(df)
}
Output
shape: (1, 2)
┌─────────┬──────────┐
│ name    │ language │
│ String  │ String   │
├─────────┼──────────┤
│ "ursus" │ "Go"     │
└─────────┴──────────┘

docs.title: SIMD kernels
docs.text:
ursus's compute kernels have SIMD versions for amd64, behind Go's simd experiment. They are optional: switch them on when you build,

GOEXPERIMENT=simd go build ./...

and without the experiment, or on another architecture, every kernel falls back to its scalar twin. That fallback is not a promise but a test: CI runs the whole suite with the experiment off on every push, as it runs it at four vector widths with it on. The flag buys speed, not correctness.

GOAMD64=v3 lets the Go compiler use AVX2, FMA and BMI in ordinary code too. ursus's own builds and benchmarks use it; any amd64 machine from the last decade has them.

docs.title: Platforms
docs.text: ursus runs wherever Go does. Its memory limit, on by default at half the memory the machine or the container allows, reads that allowance on Linux (cgroups included), macOS and Windows.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text:
ursus is at 0.6 and will stay at 0.x. Go's rule for v0 applies: a release may rename, remove or reshape an API, and the changelog lists each release's breaks with their replacements. Pin a version in your go.mod, and read the changelog before you move.

These docs are versioned too: the selector at the top of the page switches between releases, and dev is the development branch.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
This tour builds a frame, reads a file, and runs the queries most programs need. Every block of code on this site is a Go example that the test suite runs, and the output under it is what it printed.

The examples read sales.csv, eight orders:

order_id,date,region,product,qty,price
1,2026-01-03,north,apple,10,1.50
2,2026-01-03,south,apple,4,1.50
3,2026-01-04,north,pear,7,2.25
4,2026-01-05,east,pear,2,2.25
5,2026-01-05,south,fig,9,3.00
6,2026-01-06,east,apple,12,1.50
7,2026-01-07,north,fig,3,3.00
8,2026-01-07,south,pear,6,2.25

docs.title: A frame from Go values
docs.text:
Frame builds a frame from columns, and Values makes a column from a Go slice. Its type follows the slice's: []int64 is an Int64 column, []string a String one.

df, err := ursus.Frame(
    ursus.Values("city", []string{"Oslo", "Lima", "Pune"}),
    ursus.Values("population", []int64{709_000, 10_151_000, 7_764_000}),
    ursus.Values("coastal", []bool{true, true, false}),
).Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df)
Output
shape: (3, 3)
┌────────┬────────────┬─────────┐
│ city   │ population │ coastal │
│ String │ Int64      │ Bool    │
├────────┼────────────┼─────────┤
│ "Oslo" │ 709000     │ true    │
│ "Lima" │ 10151000   │ true    │
│ "Pune" │ 7764000    │ false   │
└────────┴────────────┴─────────┘

Frame gives a LazyFrame, a query. Collect runs it and gives a DataFrame, the answer.

docs.title: Reading a file
docs.text:
ScanCSV reads a CSV and infers its columns' types; an option overrides one. Here the dates become a Date:

df, err := ursus.ScanCSV("testdata/sales.csv",
    ursus.WithSchemaOverrides(map[string]ursus.DataType{"date": ursus.Date}),
).Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df)
Output
shape: (8, 6)
┌──────────┬────────────┬─────────┬─────────┬───────┬─────────┐
│ order_id │ date       │ region  │ product │ qty   │ price   │
│ Int64    │ Date       │ String  │ String  │ Int64 │ Float64 │
├──────────┼────────────┼─────────┼─────────┼───────┼─────────┤
│ 1        │ 2026-01-03 │ "north" │ "apple" │ 10    │ 1.5     │
│ 2        │ 2026-01-03 │ "south" │ "apple" │ 4     │ 1.5     │
│ 3        │ 2026-01-04 │ "north" │ "pear"  │ 7     │ 2.25    │
│ 4        │ 2026-01-05 │ "east"  │ "pear"  │ 2     │ 2.25    │
│ 5        │ 2026-01-05 │ "south" │ "fig"   │ 9     │ 3       │
│ 6        │ 2026-01-06 │ "east"  │ "apple" │ 12    │ 1.5     │
│ 7        │ 2026-01-07 │ "north" │ "fig"   │ 3     │ 3       │
│ 8        │ 2026-01-07 │ "south" │ "pear"  │ 6     │ 2.25    │
└──────────┴────────────┴─────────┴─────────┴───────┴─────────┘

ScanParquet reads Parquet the same way, and ScanCSVReader, ScanParquetBytes, ScanCSVFrom and ScanParquetFrom read from memory or from any reader you open, an object store's included.

docs.title: Selecting and filtering
docs.text:
Filter keeps the rows where an expression is true, and Select keeps or computes columns:

df, err := ursus.ScanCSV("testdata/sales.csv").
    Filter(ursus.Col("region").Eq("north")).
    Select(ursus.Col("product"), ursus.Col("qty")).
    Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df)
Output
shape: (3, 2)
┌─────────┬───────┐
│ product │ qty   │
│ String  │ Int64 │
├─────────┼───────┤
│ "apple" │ 10    │
│ "pear"  │ 7     │
│ "fig"   │ 3     │
└─────────┴───────┘

Columns are named with Col, and an expression's methods build on it: Eq, Gt, Ge, And, Or, IsNull. Methods have names because Go has no operator overloading: Col("qty").Gt(3), not qty > 3.

docs.title: Adding columns
docs.text:
WithColumns adds columns, or replaces those of the same name. When, Then and Otherwise choose a value by a condition:

df, err := ursus.ScanCSV("testdata/sales.csv").
    WithColumns(
        ursus.Col("qty").Mul(ursus.Col("price")).Alias("revenue"),
        ursus.When(ursus.Col("qty").Ge(int64(8))).Then("bulk").Otherwise("single").Alias("kind"),
    ).
    Select(ursus.Col("order_id"), ursus.Col("revenue"), ursus.Col("kind")).
    Head(4).
    Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df)
Output
shape: (4, 3)
┌──────────┬─────────┬──────────┐
│ order_id │ revenue │ kind     │
│ Int64    │ Float64 │ String   │
├──────────┼─────────┼──────────┤
│ 1        │ 15      │ "bulk"   │
│ 2        │ 6       │ "single" │
│ 3        │ 15.75   │ "single" │
│ 4        │ 4.5     │ "single" │
└──────────┴─────────┴──────────┘

docs.title: Grouping
docs.text:
GroupBy takes the keys, and Agg the aggregates to compute for each group:

df, err := ursus.ScanCSV("testdata/sales.csv").
    GroupBy(ursus.Col("product")).
    Agg(
        ursus.Col("qty").Sum().Alias("qty"),
        ursus.Col("price").Max().Alias("price"),
        ursus.Col("region").NUnique().Alias("regions"),
    ).
    Sort(ursus.Asc(ursus.Col("product"))).
    Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df)
Output
shape: (3, 4)
┌─────────┬────────┬─────────┬─────────┐
│ product │ qty    │ price   │ regions │
│ String  │ Int128 │ Float64 │ Uint64  │
├─────────┼────────┼─────────┼─────────┤
│ "apple" │ 26     │ 1.5     │ 3       │
│ "fig"   │ 12     │ 3       │ 2       │
│ "pear"  │ 15     │ 2.25    │ 3       │
└─────────┴────────┴─────────┴─────────┘

A sum of integers is an Int128, so it cannot overflow; cast it if you need an Int64. Groups come out in no promised order: sort them, or call MaintainOrder() for the order their keys first appear in.

docs.title: Joining
docs.text:
Join matches rows by keys. JoinHow picks the kind: inner by default, and left, right, full, semi, anti and cross. A row with no match on the other side takes nulls:

managers := ursus.Frame(
    ursus.Values("region", []string{"north", "south"}),
    ursus.Values("manager", []string{"Ada", "Grace"}),
)
df, err := ursus.ScanCSV("testdata/sales.csv").
    Join(managers, ursus.JoinOn(ursus.Col("region")), ursus.JoinHow(ursus.JoinLeft)).
    Select(ursus.Col("order_id"), ursus.Col("region"), ursus.Col("manager")).
    Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df)
Output
shape: (8, 3)
┌──────────┬─────────┬─────────┐
│ order_id │ region  │ manager │
│ Int64    │ String  │ String  │
├──────────┼─────────┼─────────┤
│ 1        │ "north" │ "Ada"   │
│ 2        │ "south" │ "Grace" │
│ 3        │ "north" │ "Ada"   │
│ 4        │ "east"  │ null    │
│ 5        │ "south" │ "Grace" │
│ 6        │ "east"  │ null    │
│ 7        │ "north" │ "Ada"   │
│ 8        │ "south" │ "Grace" │
└──────────┴─────────┴─────────┘

docs.title: Back into Go
docs.text:
Rows decodes a frame into a slice of structs, matching fields to columns by an ursus tag, by name, or by name ignoring case:

type sale struct {
    ID      int64  `ursus:"order_id"`
    Product string `ursus:"product"`
    Qty     int64  `ursus:"qty"`
}
df, err := ursus.ScanCSV("testdata/sales.csv").
    Filter(ursus.Col("qty").Ge(int64(9))).
    Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
sales, err := df.Rows[sale]()
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
for _, s := range sales {
    fmt.Printf("%+v\n", s)
}
Output
{ID:1 Product:apple Qty:10}
{ID:5 Product:fig Qty:9}
{ID:6 Product:apple Qty:12}

df.Column[T](name) gives one column as a typed Series[T], and df.At[T](row, name) one value and whether it was null.

docs.title: What will run
docs.text:
Explain shows the plan the optimizer made. Here the scan reads two of the file's six columns, and the Select is gone, because the scan already gives just those two:

plan, err := ursus.ScanCSV("testdata/sales.csv").
    Filter(ursus.Col("qty").Gt(int64(3))).
    Select(ursus.Col("product"), ursus.Col("qty")).
    Explain(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(plan)
Output
FILTER [(col("qty") > lit(3))]
  CSV SCAN testdata/sales.csv
    projection: [product, qty] (2/6 cols)

docs.title: API reference
docs.text:
The reference for every package, type and method is generated from the source on pkg.go.dev, for this version of ursus:

github.com/advenn/ursus@v0.6.6 on pkg.go.dev

Its doc comments say why a thing is the way it is, not only what it does, and the runnable examples beside the methods are run by go test, as this site's are.

The packages:

Package What it holds ursus frames, expressions, scans and sinks: everything a query needs ursus/dtype the type system, re-exported by ursus as ursus.Int64, ursus.Schema and the rest ursus/ursustest assertions for tests: frames equal, and golden plans ursus/i128 the 128-bit integer behind Int128 and Decimal

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text:
ursus follows Go's rule for v0: nothing is promised, and a minor version may change behaviour. Each release below therefore says what a user of the previous one can trip on, not only what is new.

ursus will stay 0.x; there will be no 1.0. So no API is frozen and none is deprecated first: a minor version renames, removes or reshapes an API whenever the result is better. From 0.6 on, each release lists its breaks, each with its replacement.

Every step of construction has an as-built record in context_files/, with the measurements behind each change. Step numbers below point at those records.

docs.title: v0.6.6 — 2026-10-19
docs.text: Everything since v0.6.5 (2026-10-15): steps 262–287. v0.6.6-scope.md set the scope: feature completeness, part 2 — namespaces and generators. Frame operations are 0.6.7 and I/O 0.6.8; feature-gaps.md lists what is missing. Step 287 checked the whole.

docs.title: Where it ends
docs.text:
• Polars' namespaces and generators:
  • generators, temporal ranges and values from their components; folds; selection by position; List().Eval;
  • the .list, .str and .dt methods that were missing, .cat on an Enum, .bin, and struct fields of several names;
  • the statistics, integers as bits, search, hashing and counts of values, run lengths and sequences, and rounding modes;
  • rolling skew, kurtosis, rank, cov and corr, ewm_sum and the ewms by time, hist and cumulative_eval.
  • Each answers as Polars 1.44.1 does, checked against its answers on the same inputs.
  • Many hold to the bit, the rounding, the moments, the ewms and hist ported from Polars' own source.
  • The exceptions: Hash, Sample and ApproxNUnique, which cannot, and the differences feature-gaps.md §9 records.
  • Each spills or streams where its pieces do. A per-row function streams a batch at a time, a reshape in a Select spills through the frame operator it is written in, and an aggregate spills with the group-by. The rolling and ewm functions stream over one partition. What refuses under a limit is listed below.
  • Nothing the benchmarks run changed:
  • the optimized plans of the 22 PDS-H and 15 h2o queries are byte-identical to v0.6.5's, once step 287 named Len() without the Alias node that showed in gb9's plan. So no timing ran, and 0.6.4's figures stand.
  • Every PDS-H answer at SF=0.1, at every step, and every h2o answer at 10,000,000 rows over Parquet match DuckDB's.

docs.title: Breaks
docs.text:
• Str().SplitN(by, n) is a Struct, fields field_0 to field_{n-1}, as Polars' splitn (270). It was a List, n <= 0 unlimited: Str().Split(by) is every part.
  • A struct's field is named after the field, as Polars names it (275): Col("s").Struct().Field("b") is b, where it was s. So WithFields of a field read sets that field, where it added one named after the struct.
  • A null bound of Clip is no bound, for its row, as Polars' None is (283). It was a null result, and a null literal bound nulled the whole column.
  • Str() refuses a Binary column, as Polars' .str does (274). It read one as text, and a text function such as Slice split its bytes as runes; Bin() has the byte functions.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Generators (263): IntRange, LinearSpace, Repeat, Ones and Zeros, a column of their own length, e.g. WithColumns(IntRange(0, Len(), 1).Alias("i")); and their per-row forms IntRanges, LinearSpaces and Expr.RepeatBy, a List a row. LinearSpace agrees with Polars' to the bit.
  • Temporal ranges (264): DateRange, DatetimeRange and TimeRange, and DateRanges, DatetimeRanges and TimeRanges a row, by an Interval or a time.Duration, each value start plus k intervals as Polars counts them.
  • Values from their components (265): MakeDate, MakeDatetime, MakeTime and MakeDuration, Polars' pl.date and its kin, from constants or expressions; FromEpoch; and BusinessDayCount with a BusinessCalendar.
  • Folds and constructors (266): ConcatList, Fold, Reduce, CumFold, CumReduce, CumSumHorizontal and Format. A fold's function builds the expression once, when the query is planned, over a selection's columns too: Fold(0, func(acc, x Expr) Expr { return acc.Add(x) }, All()).
  • Selection by position and the index functions (267): Nth, First() and Last() as column selectors; ArgWhere, ArgSortBy, and ArgSort, ArgTrue and ArgUnique on an expression, UInt32 indices, a list a group in an aggregation.
  • List().Eval and Element() (268), an expression over each list's elements: values an element, aggregates, reshapes, filters and window functions, e.g. Col("l").List().Eval(Element().Sub(Element().Mean())). And List().Agg and List().Filter.
  • The list namespace's missing methods (269): Concat, Shift, Diff, CountMatches, Any, All, Item, SampleN, SampleFraction, and SortWith for nulls last.
  • Matching, splitting and forms of strings (270): ContainsAny, ReplaceMany, ExtractMany and FindMany over many patterns, by Polars' matching rules; ExtractGroups and SplitExact, a Struct; SplitInclusive; ToTitlecase; and Normalize to NFC, NFD, NFKC or NFKD.
  • Encodings, integers in a base, and JSON (271): Str().Encode and Decode, hex or base64; ToIntegerWith(base, dtype, strict), the base a constant or a column; ReplaceN, the first n matches; ConcatStrIgnoreNulls; JsonPathMatch(path); and JsonDecode(dtype), to a type given, with Polars' conversions.
  • The temporal namespace's missing functions (272): IsoYear, Century and Millennium; BaseUtcOffset and DstOffset; WithTimeUnit; TotalMilliseconds, TotalMicroseconds and TotalNanoseconds, and every total and the second with its fraction, TotalSecondsFractional and the rest; EpochIn, EpochDays and Timestamp in a unit; IsBusinessDay and AddBusinessDays with a BusinessCalendar and a Roll; and Replace(DateTimeParts{...}), setting components.
  • The categorical namespace on an Enum (273): Cat().GetCategories, StartsWith, EndsWith, LenBytes, LenChars, Slice and Physical; and Str() reads an Enum as its text, where it refused one.
  • The binary namespace (274): Bin().Contains, StartsWith, EndsWith, Get, Head, Tail and Slice, each argument a constant or an expression; Size, Encode, Decode, and Reinterpret to a number or an instant, little- or big-endian.
  • Histograms and prefixes (286): Hist(opts...), bins by count or edges, a count or a Struct with each bin's edge and interval; CumulativeEval(body), an aggregate of Element() over each row's prefix.
  • Exponential weights (285): EwmSum, and EwmMeanBy and EwmSumBy by time, each Polars' to the bit; over the whole frame they stream under a memory limit.
  • Rolling statistics (284): RollingSkew, RollingKurtosis and RollingRank, and RollingCov and RollingCorr of two expressions. The moments are Polars' algorithm, a kurtosis Polars' to the bit.
  • Numeric odds (283): Round(decimals, RoundHalfToEven), Polars' default mode; Truncate(decimals); RoundSigFigs(digits); Cot(); ClipLower and ClipUpper. Rounding is Polars' algorithm, so each answer is Polars' to the bit.
  • Sequences (282): Append(other, upcast), ExtendConstant(value, n), SampleN, SampleFraction and Shuffle(seed), each a column of its own length in a Select and a list a group in an aggregation.
  • Run lengths (281): RleID(), a window function, and Rle(), a Struct of each run's length and value.
  • Counts of values (280): UniqueCounts() and ValueCounts(sort, normalize, name...), a Struct of each value and its count, a column of its own length in a Select and a list a group in an aggregation.
  • Search, peaks and hashing (279): SearchSorted(value, side, descending), IndexOf, PeakMax, PeakMin and Hash(seed), each comparing in the total order Sort uses, NaN above every number, as Polars'.
  • Integers as bits (278): And, Or, Xor and Not of integers are their bits', at their common type, as Polars' &, |, ^ and ~; a Go integer beside one keeps its type where it fits. A Boolean beside an integer is refused.
  • Entropy, mode and Spearman's correlation (277): Entropy(base, normalize); Mode(maintainOrder), a column of its own length or a list a group; and CorrSpearman(a, b).
  • Skew, kurtosis and small aggregates (276): Skew(bias) and Kurtosis(fisher, bias), kept online and merged pairwise; BitwiseAnd, BitwiseOr and BitwiseXor of integers or Booleans; NanMin and NanMax; HasNulls, IsEmpty, ApproxNUnique (exact) and Dot.
  • Struct().Field of several names (275), or a regex between ^ and $, or "*": a column a field, in the struct's order, as Polars' struct.field.

docs.title: Fixes
docs.text:
• A list's eval over an aggregate in a Select, Col("a").Implode().List().Eval(...), failed as an internal error (271).
  • Len() is named len, as Polars' pl.len() is; in most plans it was named literal (273). Alias of an alias now replaces the name. Since step 287 the name is OutputName's, not an Alias node's, so every plan that holds Len() renders as at v0.6.5.
  • Unnest().Suffix(...) keeps its suffix (275); each field's name undid it.

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text:
As v0.6.5's, except:

  • Refused under a memory limit, each by name:
  • CorrSpearman and Mode in a group-by past the limit: their per-group pairs and values do not spill;
  • RleID and Rle over a partition larger than the limit;
  • SampleN, SampleFraction, Shuffle and Hist in a Select, which implode the column, as implode refuses;
  • CumulativeEval over a partition larger than the limit;
  • a generator whose argument is an aggregate of the frame, beside a string column, such as WithColumns(IntRange(0, Len(), 1)). WithRowIndex streams.
  • Last bits:
  • a rolling var, std, skew, kurtosis, cov or corr streamed under a limit can differ from the answer in memory;
  • a float aggregate's depend on the thread count, Sum's and Var's as the new moments'; a spilled run is the one-thread run's.
  • Refused where Polars answers:
  • a window inside a window, Col("a").Shift(1).CumSum();
  • an aggregate inside an aggregate's input;
  • CumulativeEval in GroupBy(...).Agg, as every window is.
  • .arr waits for an Array type, in a release of types after I/O.
  • A count reads every column: Select(Len()) over Parquet projects them all; Polars reads none.

docs.title: v0.6.5 — 2026-10-15
docs.text: Everything since v0.6.4 (2026-10-14): steps 248–261. v0.6.5-scope.md set the scope: feature completeness, part 1 — the bugs, and the expression model. The rest of 0.6 is feature completeness, and 0.7 performance; feature-gaps.md lists what is missing. Step 261 checked the whole.

docs.title: Where it ends
docs.text:
• Expressions work where Polars' do. An aggregate is a scalar in Select, WithColumns and Filter. Expr.Filter is an aggregate's input. A length-changing expression is a list a group in an aggregation, and a column of its own length in Select and WithColumns. Arguments take expressions, and a Go slice is a List literal. Explode and Unnest are expressions, as DropNulls and DropNans became.
  • Each answers as Polars 1.44.1 does, checked against its answers on the same inputs, but for the differences feature-gaps.md §9 records.
  • Each spills or streams where its pieces do: a broadcast aggregate as a window, a filtered aggregate through the same accumulators, a column of another length as a plan of its own over the frame. A group's values in an aggregation are held by its implode, which refuses past the limit, as it did.
  • Nothing the benchmarks run changed: the optimized plans of the 22 PDS-H and 15 h2o queries are byte-identical to v0.6.4's, so no timing ran; 0.6.4's figures stand. Every PDS-H answer at SF=0.1, at every step, and every h2o answer at 2,000,000 rows match DuckDB's.

docs.title: Breaks
docs.text:
• List().Get, and Str()'s Contains, StartsWith, EndsWith, StripPrefix, StripSuffix, Split, Replace and ReplaceAll, are generic methods now, over a constant or an Expr. A call compiles as before; a method value needs its type argument: l.Get[int], not l.Get. IsIn, OffsetBy and Lit were generic already and take a wider type set.
  • Expr.Explode, Unnest, DropNulls and DropNans no longer refuse; code that relied on the refusal to catch a mistake gets an answer.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text: • lf.FillNull(ursus.FillForward) fills by the strategy (249). It filled every null with the constant 2: FillStrategy is a uint8, so it was taken for a value. Expr.FillNullWith(strategy) did the same. With no subset, forward and backward fill every column, min and max every ordered one, and zero, one and mean every numeric one; Polars fills a String with "" and a Bool with false for zero, and refuses a String for one and mean.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Dt().Date() and Dt().Time() (249), Polars' dt.date and dt.time: the date and time of day on the column's zone's wall clock. Cast(Date) reads the UTC one, as Polars' cast does.
  • An aggregate in Select, WithColumns and Filter is a scalar (250), as in Polars: Select(Col("x"), Col("x").Sum()) gives each row the total, WithColumns(Col("x").Sub(Col("x").Mean())) centres x, and Filter(Col("x").Gt(Col("x").Mean())) keeps the rows above the mean. A Select of aggregates, with or without literals, is one row. It was refused. The broadcast streams past a memory limit.
  • A window in Filter (250), SQL's QUALIFY: Filter(Col("x").Sum().Over(Col("g")).Gt(10)). It was refused.
  • Expr.Filter as an aggregate's input (251), a conditional aggregate: Col("a").Filter(Col("b").Gt(0)).Sum(), in a group-by, a window, a rolling or dynamic group, and as a scalar. The aggregate reads only the rows that pass, so Len counts them. Anywhere else a filter is refused for now.
  • Sort, SortDesc, Head, Tail, Slice, Reverse, Unique, DropNulls and Get on an expression (252), as Polars has them: in an aggregation a list a group, and an aggregate over one a value, Col("a").Head(2).Sum(), there and in Select, WithColumns, Filter and .Over. Expr.DropNulls was a refusal. Alone outside an aggregation they are refused for now.
  • SortBy, SortByDesc, GatherEvery and DropNans on an expression, and median, std, var and quantile over any of them (253). Expr.DropNans was a refusal. The list namespace gains Median, Std, Var, Quantile, DropNans, GatherEvery, SortBy and SortByDesc.
  • IsIn(Col("tags")), a value in each row's own list, and List().Get and List().Contains of an expression, a per-row index and value (254). IsIn now takes Operands, and Get an int or an Expr.
  • String patterns as expressions (255): Contains, StartsWith, EndsWith, StripPrefix, StripSuffix and Split take a pattern a row, and Replace and ReplaceAll a value a row, inserted as written. A null replacement value gives null, where Polars keeps the string.
  • Dt().OffsetBy of an expression (256): an offset a row, a String such as "1mo2d". One that does not parse, or that the type cannot hold, is an error naming its row.
  • List literals (257): Lit([]int64{1, 2}) and the other slices are one List value, e.g. Col("x").IsIn(Lit([]int64{1, 2})). And Expr.Gather in an aggregation, by a List literal or a column of indices.
  • Length-changing expressions in Select (258): a reshape or an Expr.Filter is a column of its own length, e.g. Select(Col("a").Sort(), Col("b").Head(3)) is refused for its two lengths and Select(Col("a").Head(3), Col("b").Sum()) is three rows. Each is a plan of its own over the frame, so it spills as the frame-level operation does.
  • WithColumns takes them at the frame's height, and Expr.Explode is an expression (259), in Select, in an aggregation and under an aggregate; it was a refusal.
  • Expr.Unnest (260): a struct's fields, a column each named after its field, in Select, WithColumns and under an operation, as Polars' struct.unnest(); it was a refusal. StructExpr.Unnest spells it as Polars does.

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text:
As v0.6.4's, except:

  • Of the expression model, each refused by name:
  • IsIn(Col("b").Implode()), membership among a column's values: 0.7's scalar subqueries;
  • a length-changing expression in Filter;
  • Gather in Select;
  • a reshape of a selection of several columns, Col("a", "b").Sort();
  • DropNans of a column that is not a float, and Explode of one that is not a List, where Polars returns them as they were.
  • A Select of literals alone is a row for each of the frame's rows; Polars' is one row.
  • A column of another length in Select reads the frame again: each is a plan of its own over it. A frame that joins, aggregates or sorts is computed once and replayed; a scan is read once a plan.

docs.title: v0.6.4 — 2026-10-14
docs.text: Everything since v0.6.3 (2026-10-12): steps 234–247. v0.6.4-scope.md set the scope: out of core, the leftovers — what still refuses under a memory budget, made to spill or stream. Step 247 measured the whole.

docs.title: Where it ends
docs.text:
• Every window function streams past a memory limit, over one huge partition too; a rolling window by time holds the rows of its period. Keyed Rolling and GroupByDynamic hand their answer out. n_unique, and a median, quantile or n_unique in a window or a temporal group, spill their values; a large top-k spills.
  • Out of core, measured: each new path under a tenth of its input gives the answer it gives without a limit, the same to the byte, peaking at 1.01 to 2.11 times the limit (step 247 §3).
  • Against v0.6.3, both built alike and alternated: level. PDS-H at SF=1 takes 1.4% less wall time by geomean and 0.4% more CPU, at SF=0.1 2% less; h2o's gb1, gb4, gb5 and j1 move by −8% to +2%. 0.6.4 changed what happens past a limit, and these run without one.
  • Against Polars, in one session, every answer validated against DuckDB's:
suite ursus Polars ratio at v0.6.3 PDS-H SF=1 158 ms 79 ms 2.01× 1.94× PDS-H SF=0.1 20 ms 9 ms 2.29× 1.82× h2o 10M, Parquet 697 ms 531 ms 1.31× 1.20× h2o 10M, CSV 1,784 ms 1,088 ms 1.64× 1.77×

The builds are level, so the ratios move with the session: both engines ran h2o faster than in 0.6.3's, which was short of memory, Polars by more over Parquet and ursus by more over CSV. - CI's race job, which had timed out since step 237, has twenty minutes, and its heaviest budget tests run smaller under the race detector (244).

docs.title: Out of core
docs.text:
• A window with an order_by streams over one huge partition (235), with no partition_by or over one hot key: its rows' order keys and inputs are sorted, the functions walked over them, and the answers sorted back beside the rows. It refused.
  • A reversed cumulative function and a backward fill with no limit stream over one huge partition (236), walked backward through a reverse of that stream. They refused.
  • Rank, every method, streams over one huge partition (237), in its child's order: max and average from the peer group's first position counted both ways. It refused.
  • Interpolation, linear and nearest, streams over one huge partition (238), from a walk each way finding the values on either side and their positions. It refused.
  • A sort merges its spilled runs as they gather, sixteen of one level into one of the next (239), so its final merge holds a batch of fewer than sixteen runs a level. A window's sorted pass peaked at 6.7× its limit and now at 1.2×.
  • A window with no partition_by beside a keyed one spills (240), its keyless functions one more pass of the keyed spill. It refused. Of windows over one huge partition, only a rolling window by time still refuses.
  • n_unique over a few huge groups, or with no key, spills its values (241), as sorted runs of their bytes, counted as they merge back. It refused. Implode, whose answer is every value, still does.
  • A median, quantile or n_unique in a window spills its values over one huge partition (242), as a group-by's does. It refused. A run of spilled values, a group-by's too, is now written a batch at a time, so the merge back holds a batch of each run rather than a chunk of 8,192 values.
  • Keyed Rolling and GroupByDynamic hand their answer out (243) as their windows close, and a sort that spills puts it in bucket order. They held every window, and refused past the limit. In memory a keyed group is a little slower: over 2,000,000 rows under 1,000 keys, +4% rolling and +13% dynamic.
  • A median, quantile or n_unique in Rolling or GroupByDynamic spills its values (244), keyed or not, as a group-by's does. Windows that overlap hold a value for every (window, row) pair, many times their input, and refused past the limit. Implode still does.
  • Sort(...).Head(k) with a large k spills (245): past the limit its best k rows go to disk as runs, and the first k of their merge are the answer, ties in input order. It held them past the limit.
  • A rolling window by time streams over one huge partition (246), in a sorted pass by its by, each function's state carried from batch to batch so that the answers match the in-memory ones to the bit. It refused. It holds the rows of its period, and refuses, naming the period, only when one period is past the limit. Every window function now streams past the limit.

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text:
As v0.6.3's, except:

  • Operators that do not spill, each failing under a budget with an error naming itself:
  • a rolling window by time one of whose periods holds more rows than the limit;
  • implode over a group, a window partition or a temporal window larger than the limit: its answer is every value;
  • join_asof's read-ahead: a left by-key the right side lacks reads that side to its end and holds it;
  • a dynamic group's long gap in its index makes every empty window in it at once, under the window ceiling.
  • A keyed Rolling or GroupByDynamic is a little slower in memory, +4% and +13% over 2,000,000 rows under 1,000 keys: its windows go out in segments and are put in bucket order at the end.
  • Speed: 2.01× Polars on PDS-H at SF=1. The widest gaps are q12 at 4.3×, q19 at 3.5× and q16 at 2.9×; over h2o, gb4 at 2.3× over Parquet and 3.1× over CSV, the joins at 1.7 to 2.1×.
  • Memory: with no limit set, h2o's gb10 peaks at 7.7 GB over Parquet and 6.4 GB over CSV; Polars' highest is 5.0 GB.
  • A large top-k is slower in memory than under a limit: the best half of two million rows takes 1.35 s as a heap, and 0.42 s as spilled sorted runs.

docs.title: v0.6.3 — 2026-10-12
docs.text: Everything since v0.6.2 (2026-10-12): steps 213–232. v0.6.3-scope.md set the scope: wall-time speed, out-of-core, and features. Each step was timed against 0.6.2's code, alternated in one session, and step 232 measured the whole.

docs.title: Where it ends
docs.text:
• Against v0.6.2, both built alike and alternated over PDS-H at SF=1: 7.6% less wall time by geomean, 2.2% more CPU, the Parquet reader decoding ahead. q11 takes 30% less time, q4 22%, q15, q21 and q12 15 to 17%. Over h2o, gb1 takes 31% less, gb4 24%, gb5 8%.
  • The scope's claims: PDS-H at least 7% faster by wall time, no query slower beyond about 5%, and q1's and gb4's peak memory within +100 MB, met; gb4 at least 35% faster, not met, at 24%: it is bound by this laptop's four cores.
  • Against Polars, in one session, every answer validated against DuckDB's:
suite ursus Polars ratio at v0.6.2 PDS-H SF=1 148 ms 76 ms 1.94× 2.07× PDS-H SF=0.1 18 ms 10 ms 1.82× 2.76× h2o 10M, Parquet 928 ms 774 ms 1.20× 1.52× h2o 10M, CSV 2,535 ms 1,434 ms 1.77× 1.65×

The laptop was short of memory, and both engines ran h2o slower than in 0.6.2's session, by different amounts. The h2o ratios measure that session, and the alternated runs what 0.6.3 changed: faster than 0.6.2 over Parquet and CSV. - Out of core: tail, hstack, a keyless WhereExists with a predicate, a median or quantile over a few huge groups, and ewm and a reversed cum_count over one huge partition, each past a limit that refused it before. - Features: the list namespace's set operations, Gather, ToStruct, NUnique, ArgMin and ArgMax; six horizontal reductions; Replace and its strict forms; rolling median and quantile; eager Pivot and Transpose; DaysInMonth, Combine, RenameFields and JsonEncode. Each answers as Polars does, checked against its answers, except where its docs say otherwise.

docs.title: Faster
docs.text:
• The Parquet reader reads ahead (214). A row group not at the head decoded three batches and waited, so most of each decoded only once it was the head, one at a time. Each now decodes ahead while what the workers hold stays under a read-ahead of a thirty-second of the memory limit, at most 256 MiB. h2o gb1 takes 28% less time, PDS-H q6 10% and q1 8%; peak memory grows by up to about 90 MB.
  • A sum or mean of an integer of 32 bits or fewer adds in int64 (215), folding into its exact 128-bit sum every 2³⁰ rows and at the end, where every value was widened to 128 bits first. h2o gb4 takes 15% less time, gb5 8%.

docs.title: Out of core
docs.text:
• Tail spills (217). The last rows it holds go to run files past the budget, the oldest dropped as later rows cover them, and come back in order a batch at a time. It refused.
  • Hstack streams (218), pairing a batch of each frame at a time, sliced to the fewest rows any has left. It held every frame whole, and refused. Frames of different heights are still refused, after the rows paired before.
  • A WhereExists or WhereNotExists of a predicate alone spills (219): a keyless Semi or Anti join with a residual writes its build side to a file and reads it for each probe batch until each row is decided. It refused.
  • A median or quantile over a huge group spills its values (220): over a few hot keys, or over no key, past the budget its values go to sorted run files, which are merged as they gather and read back in one pass at the end. A group-by partitions keys, never the values of one, so it refused. n_unique and implode over a hot key still refuse.
  • Ewm functions and a reversed cum_count stream over one huge partition (221), with no partition_by or for one key of a partition_by: an ewm carries its running state from batch to batch, and a reversed count counts down from the rows written. They refused.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• List().NUnique(), List().ArgMin() and List().ArgMax() (222), each the column aggregate over a list's elements: Uint64s, nulls skipped and NaN the largest, as the aggregates have them. A null list is null, an empty list counts 0 and has no position.
  • List().SetUnion, SetIntersection, SetDifference and SetSymmetricDifference, and List().Gather(indices, nullOnOOB) (223), each taking a second List column, in Polars' order and with its equality: a null element is a value, NaN meets NaN, −0 meets +0. An Int64 list against a Float64 list is refused, as a join of the two is.
  • List().ToStruct(names...) and Struct().RenameFields(names...) (224). A list's first elements become named fields, null where it is shorter; a null list is a null struct. Renaming must name every field, which Polars only warns about.
  • MaxHorizontal, MinHorizontal, SumHorizontal, MeanHorizontal, AnyHorizontal and AllHorizontal (225): each row's reduction across expressions, max to mean answering as the column aggregates do over the row's values, any and all as Kleene's Or and And.
  • Replace, ReplaceStrict and ReplaceOr (226), a value map matching as IsIn does. Replace keeps unmatched values and types as the matching When chain would; ReplaceStrict refuses an unmatched value; ReplaceOr gives unmatched values and nulls a default.
  • RollingMedian, RollingQuantile, RollingMedianBy and RollingQuantileBy (227): a window's median and quantile, by rows or by time, centred or not, and streamed past the memory limit with no partition_by.
  • Eager DataFrame methods (228) for fifteen lazy operations that had none: Slice, Limit, DropNulls, FillNull, FillNan, TopK, BottomK, HStack, VStack, JoinAsOf, MergeSorted, Explode, Unnest, WithRowIndex and Remove; GroupBy, GroupByDynamic and Rolling start the lazy builder.
  • DataFrame.Pivot and DataFrame.Transpose (229), eager only since their columns come from the data: a pivot in Polars' row and column order and naming, refusing a cell of two values without an aggregate; a transpose at the type every column meets at.
  • Dt().DaysInMonth() and Dt().Combine(t) (230): a month's length, and a day with a Time of day, read and written on the column's own wall clock.
  • Struct().JsonEncode() (231): each struct as a JSON object, floats in their shortest form, NaN as null, strings escaped, temporals and Decimals as the text their String cast gives.

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text:
As v0.6.2's, except:

  • Operators that do not spill, each failing under a budget with an error naming itself:
  • a window, with or without a partition_by, whose one partition is larger than the limit and that computes a rank, an interpolation, a reversed cumulative function other than cum_count, an unlimited backward fill or a rolling window by time, or that is ordered;
  • n_unique and implode over a few very large groups.
  • What streams but holds its answer: a keyed Rolling or GroupByDynamic, which gives its answer per bucket.
  • Spilling a keyed window needs about 128 KiB for its partition writers, past any limit set below that.
  • Speed: 1.94× Polars on PDS-H at SF=1. The widest gaps are q7 at 3.9×, q19 at 3.3×, q16 at 3.2× and q15 at 3.1×; over h2o, the joins at 1.6 to 2.0×. On this four-core laptop the queries the reader no longer waits on are bound by the CPU.
  • Memory: with no limit set, h2o's gb10 peaks at 6.8 GB over Parquet and 8.2 GB over CSV; Polars at 4.7 and 5.1 GB. The read-ahead adds up to about 90 MB to a Parquet query's peak.
  • Pivot and Transpose are eager only, their columns coming from the data, which a lazy plan's schema cannot wait for.

docs.title: v0.6.2 — 2026-10-12
docs.text: Everything since v0.6.1 (2026-10-11): steps 201–212. v0.6.2-scope.md set the scope: speed and out-of-core, continued. Each step was timed against 0.6.1's code, alternated in one session, and step 208 measured the whole.

docs.title: Where it ends
docs.text:
• Against v0.6.1, both built alike and alternated over PDS-H at SF=1: 8.6% less CPU by geomean, 2.5% less wall time. q7, q21 and q4 take 23% less CPU and 11 to 12% less time, q17 19% and 10%.
  • The scope's claims were q7 and q21 at least 20% faster, and PDS-H at SF=1 at least 5%: met by CPU, not by wall time. The work removed was per-row hash work that ran on every core at once.
  • Against Polars, in one session, every answer validated against DuckDB's:
suite ursus Polars ratio at v0.6.1 PDS-H SF=1 159 ms 77 ms 2.07× 2.16× PDS-H SF=0.1 24 ms 9 ms 2.76× 2.43× h2o 10M, Parquet 822 ms 541 ms 1.52× 1.51× h2o 10M, CSV 1,764 ms 1,071 ms 1.65× 1.70×

At SF=0.1 ursus is as it was, 24.6 to 24.1 ms, and Polars ran faster, 10.1 to 8.7 ms. - Out of core: reverse, an unkeyed Rolling or GroupByDynamic, and one partition of a keyed window, each past a limit that refused or held its answer before. Reverse passes under a tenth of its input, and the unkeyed Rolling too at batches of 2,048: it holds a batch's worth, about 700 KB at 8,192 rows.

docs.title: Faster
docs.text:
• A runtime filter tests a dense key against a bitmap (202), a bit for each value in the join keys' range, where it looked each probe row up in the join's hash tables. q8, q7, q5 and q21 take 10 to 19% less CPU.
  • A join finds a dense integer key by index (203): a slot for each value in the build keys' range, holding its id, where the probe hashed every row. q17 takes 12% less CPU, q3 and q7 4% less.
  • A join's dense build skips the hash tables (204). A deferred build whose integer keys are dense routes them by their place in the range, and fills that index directly, in parallel; it hashed every row into partitioned tables. q21 takes 18% less CPU and 13% less time, q4 20% and 11%.
  • A group-by on one String or Binary key hashes the values themselves (205), read in place from the column, where it encoded each first. h2o gb1 takes 31% less CPU and 23% less time over Parquet.
  • A short quoted CSV field is scanned once (211), where its line endings were counted and its carriage returns searched for by two more calls. h2o gb1 and gb3 over CSV take 7 to 9% less CPU and 6% less time.

docs.title: Out of core
docs.text:
• Reverse spills (206). Past the budget it writes what it holds to a run file, and gives the runs back last to first, each read whole, so it holds one at a time. It refused. In memory it no longer concatenates its input before reversing it.
  • Rolling and GroupByDynamic with no key hand their windows out as they close (207), a batch's worth at a time, where they held their whole answer to the end. A 30-minute rolling group over 300,000 rows peaks at 0.73 MB, where it peaked at about 20 MB; over 200,000 it answers under a tenth of its input. With a key the answer is still held: it is given per bucket.
  • A window's one partition larger than the limit streams (209) when every function in it needs only a bounded part of it: its rows go to one file and are read back, as a window with no partition_by has since 197, and the other keys spill as before. It refused. A rank, an ewm or an ordered window over it still does.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• A join's key tables are on the memory ledger while it probes (204). The account was rebased at the end of the build without them, so a join probing 200,000 keys under-reported by 6 to 10 MB.
  • A spilled window keeps to its limit (210). Merging its partition files' answers, it held each file's whole answer, so the input: 971 KB under a 121 KB limit over 20,000 rows. It holds a batch across the files now.

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text:
As v0.6.1's, except:

  • Operators that do not spill, each failing under a budget with an error naming itself:
  • hstack and tail;
  • a window, with or without a partition_by, whose one partition is larger than the limit and that computes a rank, an ewm function, an interpolation, a reversed cumulative function, an unlimited backward fill or a rolling window by time, or that is ordered;
  • a join with no keys and a residual, a WhereExists of a predicate alone;
  • quantile-like aggregates over a few very large groups.
  • What streams but holds its answer: a keyed Rolling or GroupByDynamic, which gives its answer per bucket.
  • Spilling a keyed window needs about 128 KiB for its partition writers, past any limit set below that.
  • Speed: 2.07× Polars on PDS-H at SF=1. The widest gaps are q15 at 3.6×, q19 and q16 at 3.5×. A string group-by of many groups (h2o gb3) is bound by memory across the workers' tables.
  • Memory: with no limit set, h2o's gb10 peaks at 5.3 to 9.1 GB, noisy by the collector's timing; Polars at 4.5 to 5.2 GB.

docs.title: v0.6.1 — 2026-10-11
docs.text: Everything since v0.6.0 (2026-10-11): steps 191–200. v0.6.1-scope.md set the scope: speed where the profile points, and out-of-core. Each step was timed against v0.6.0's code, alternated in one session, and step 200 measured the whole.

docs.title: Where it ends
docs.text:
• Against v0.6.0, both built alike and alternated over PDS-H at SF=1: 10.9% less wall time by geomean, 3.5% less CPU. q19 takes 45% less, q12 27%, q1 25%.
  • Against Polars, in one session, every answer validated against DuckDB's:
suite ursus Polars ratio at v0.6.0 PDS-H SF=1 168 ms 78 ms 2.16× 2.32× PDS-H SF=0.1 25 ms 10 ms 2.43× 2.56× h2o 10M, Parquet 796 ms 528 ms 1.51× 1.61× h2o 10M, CSV 1,886 ms 1,110 ms 1.70× 1.81×
  • Out of core: a forward or nearest JoinAsOf, a cross join, GroupByDynamic, Rolling, and a window with no partition_by, each past a limit that refused it before. h2o's gb10 and j5 pass under 3 GB, peaking at 2.74 to 2.91 GB.

docs.title: Faster
docs.text:
• The Parquet reader decodes its own pages (192) for a flat column of an integer, float or byte-array type, PLAIN or dictionary-encoded: definition levels as runs, and each dictionary string copied once, short ones as two words. q19 and q12 take about 22% less wall time, and h2o's j2, j3 and gb1 over Parquet 10 to 15% less. Every other chunk reads through arrow-go as before.
  • The CSV reader cuts its blocks speculatively (199), after the first line ending past a block's size, and lets each block's parse prove the cut. A block that does not end cleanly sends the rest of the stream back to be cut exactly, as before, so answers and errors are unchanged. The splitter had been 60% of h2o gb1's read over CSV, on one goroutine; h2o over CSV takes 5 to 12% less wall time.
  • A string conjunct runs once per dictionary value, in the Parquet reader (193). l_shipmode IN ('AIR', 'AIR REG'), ==, StartsWith, a regexp, any row-local expression of one String or Binary column, is evaluated on each row group's dictionary, and the rows it rejects are dropped before their strings are copied. The Filter above still decides. q19 takes 27% less wall time than at step 192, and q8, q10 and q12 3 to 8% less.

docs.title: Out of core
docs.text:
• A forward or nearest JoinAsOf streams both sides (194), as a backward one has since step 183: it holds a row a by-key and the right rows it reads ahead to find a by-key's next one. Over a 300,000-row right side every strategy peaks under 1 MiB, where forward held the right side twice. A left by-key the right side lacks still reads that side to its end, and is charged for it.
  • GroupByDynamic and Rolling stream their input (196), where they buffered it whole: each row is given to its windows as it arrives, and a rolling group keeps only the rows a window yet to come reaches. Over 300,000 rows, a dynamic group's peak falls from 7.5 MB to 0.4 MB. A rolling group's answer is a row an input row, and it now holds that rather than its input as well: 10 MB from 17 MB.
  • A window with no partition_by spills (197) when every function in it needs only a bounded part of the frame: aggregates broadcast to the rows, cumulative functions, Shift and Diff, fills with a limit, a forward fill without one, and rolling windows of rows. Its rows go to one file and are read back a batch at a time. Rank, ewm, interpolation and an ordered window still refuse.
  • A cross join spills (195). Past its limit its build side goes to disk whole, and each probe row reads it back, in the in-memory order. It refused before, and so did JoinWhere, a cross join under a filter. A join with no keys and a residual, a WhereExists of a predicate alone, still refuses.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text: • A Parquet page whose RLE run holds a value wider than its bit width is refused as corrupt (192), found by fuzzing the new decoder.

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text:
As v0.6.0's, except:

  • Operators that do not spill, each failing under a budget with an error naming itself:
  • reverse, hstack and tail;
  • a window with no partition_by that computes a rank, an ewm function, an interpolation, a reversed cumulative function, an unlimited backward fill or a rolling window by time, or that is ordered;
  • one partition of a keyed window larger than the limit;
  • a join with no keys and a residual, a WhereExists of a predicate alone;
  • quantile-like aggregates over a few very large groups.
  • What streams but holds its answer: Rolling and GroupByDynamic hold their windows' state, which is their answer, until the end.
  • What streams but may read ahead: a forward or nearest JoinAsOf whose left by-key the right side lacks reads the right side to its end.
  • Speed: 2.16× Polars on PDS-H at SF=1. The widest gaps are q7 at 3.6×, q16 and q17 at 3.4×, and q15 at 3.3×. ZSTD decompression is 17 to 48% of the widest, and has no faster pure Go decoder.
  • Memory: with no limit set, h2o's gb10 peaks at 6.76 GB over CSV, Polars at 5.13 GB.

docs.title: v0.6.0 — 2026-10-11
docs.text: Everything since v0.5.0 (2026-10-09): steps 156–190. v0.6-scope.md set the scope: speed, the features 0.5 left, and robustness. audit-0.6-midpoint.md took stock after step 165. Each step below was timed against the one before it, and step 189 measured the whole against v0.5.0 and against Polars.

docs.title: Where it ends
docs.text:
The scope claimed ursus within 3× of Polars on PDS-H at SF=1, and at least 20% faster than v0.5.0 on it. Both are met. Measured on 2026-10-11, at c6aa77d (step 189):
